subChunks.title: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, and Referential Integrity
subChunks.hookHtml: Primary and foreign keys are the structural spine of a relational database. Understanding their full syntax and the cascade options that govern deletion is essential for production schema design.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
PRIMARY KEY syntax

-- Single column (inline):
id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY

-- Multi-column PK (table-level — required for composite keys):
CREATE TABLE quest_completions (
  apprentice_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  quest_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (apprentice_id, quest_id)
);

FOREIGN KEY syntax

-- Inline:
mentor_id INTEGER REFERENCES mentors(id)

-- Table-level (more control):
FOREIGN KEY (mentor_id) REFERENCES mentors(id)
  ON DELETE SET NULL
  ON UPDATE CASCADE

ON DELETE options

  • RESTRICT / NO ACTION — default; prevent deletion of the parent row if children exist
  • CASCADE — automatically delete child rows when parent is deleted
  • SET NULL — set the foreign key to NULL when parent is deleted (column must allow NULL)
  • SET DEFAULT — set to column's default value

Surrogate vs natural keys

A surrogate key is a generated integer with no business meaning (most common). A natural key is a real attribute that happens to be unique (e.g. email, ISBN). Surrogate keys are more stable — natural key values can change.

storyBeats.text: 'What happens to an apprentice's completions when the quest is deleted?' The Archivist points to the cascade option.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: ON DELETE CASCADE means delete the children automatically. ON DELETE SET NULL means blank out the reference. ON DELETE RESTRICT means refuse — never delete the parent while children exist. Choose deliberately. CASCADE is convenient but can silently erase data if the delete was accidental.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Cascade analysis

Given the schema below, answer: (1) what happens to quest_completions rows when a quest is deleted with ON DELETE CASCADE, (2) what happens to apprentice rows when a mentor is deleted with ON DELETE SET NULL.

apprentices(id PK, name, mentor_id FK → mentors(id) ON DELETE SET NULL)
quest_completions(id PK, apprentice_id FK → apprentices(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, quest_id FK → quests(id) ON DELETE CASCADE)
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) ON DELETE CASCADE on quest_completions.quest_id: when a quest is deleted, all quest_completion rows referencing that quest are automatically deleted. This is appropriate if completions are meaningless without the quest.

(2) ON DELETE SET NULL on apprentices.mentor_id: when a mentor is deleted, the mentor_id column in affected apprentice rows is set to NULL. The apprentice rows themselves are not deleted — they remain, but are now unassigned.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Write a CREATE TABLE for quest_completions with a composite primary key (apprentice_id, quest_id) and foreign keys to both apprentices and quests. Use ON DELETE CASCADE for both foreign keys.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
CREATE TABLE quest_completions (
  apprentice_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES apprentices(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  quest_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES quests(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  score         INTEGER,
  completed_at  TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (apprentice_id, quest_id)
);
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL do, and give an example of when each would be the right choice.

questions.prompt: What does ON DELETE CASCADE mean on a foreign key?
options: When the referenced parent row is deleted, all child rows referencing it are automatically deleted too
When the parent is deleted, the foreign key column is set to NULL
When the parent is deleted, the child rows are moved to an archive table
Prevents deletion of the parent if children exist
questions.answer: When the referenced parent row is deleted, all child rows referencing it are automatically deleted too
questions.explanation: CASCADE propagates the delete to children. Delete a quest → all quest_completion rows for that quest are deleted automatically.

questions.prompt: What is the default behaviour if ON DELETE is not specified for a foreign key?
options: RESTRICT / NO ACTION — the parent delete is rejected if children exist
SET NULL — the foreign key is set to NULL
The delete succeeds silently, leaving orphaned child rows
questions.answer: RESTRICT / NO ACTION — the parent delete is rejected if children exist
questions.explanation: The SQL default is RESTRICT (or NO ACTION, which is semantically equivalent in most engines). The engine refuses to delete a parent row that still has dependent children.

questions.prompt: Why use a composite primary key `PRIMARY KEY (user_id, quest_id)` in a junction table?
options: It enforces that the same user cannot complete the same quest more than once (if one completion per pair is the rule)
It prevents NULL values in both columns
It allows NULL in one column only
questions.answer: It enforces that the same user cannot complete the same quest more than once (if one completion per pair is the rule)
questions.explanation: A composite PK ensures uniqueness on the combination. (user_id=1, quest_id=5) can exist only once. This enforces the business rule that each user can have at most one completion record per quest.

questions.prompt: Why are surrogate keys (auto-generated integers) generally preferred over natural keys (e.g. email address) as primary keys?
options: Natural key values can change (e.g. a user changes their email), which would cascade updates to all foreign key references
Surrogate keys are smaller and faster to index
Surrogate keys are required by the SQL standard
questions.answer: Natural key values can change (e.g. a user changes their email), which would cascade updates to all foreign key references
questions.explanation: Natural keys tie the PK to a real-world value that can change. Changing email requires updating every table that foreign-keys to it. Surrogate keys are stable identifiers that never need to change regardless of business data changes.
